6	# Verify in production
7	
8	A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
9	that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
10	repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
11	unattended: an automatic check, end to end, that the run can make from this repository.
12	Where it cannot, the answer is almost always to file nothing and say the change is
13	unverified; asking a person is a rare exception, and no automatic check existing is not
14	on its own enough to earn one.
15	
16	## When it fires: after the merge, never before
17	
18	**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
19	calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
20	when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.
21	
22	The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
23	under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:
24	
25	- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. (1)
26	- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
27	  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
28	  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
29	  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
30	  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
31	  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.
32	
33	So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
34	merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.
35	
36	## First: does this file anything at all?
37	
38	Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:
39	
40	1. **Can you watch it work in this session — now, or after a wait you can sit through?**
41	   Then do that and file nothing — the bar is "could you", not "did you already". If it
42	   becomes readable inside the session you are in, waiting for it is cheaper than every
43	   mechanism below. (2)
44	2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
45	   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
46	   that comes back.
47	3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
48	   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
49	4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
50	   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
51	   its rules — that is what you file.
52	
53	The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
54	filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.
55	And the test above only files point assertions: when the merge completes a **larger element** —
56	one that earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue — the ~week-later review of how the
57	whole design fared is [production-retrospective](../production-retrospective/SKILL.md)'s
58	separate call, made beside this one.
59	
60	## Second: which runner can read it? If neither, file nothing
61	
62	There are two runners, and the artifact's address decides which one a verification
63	gets — never preference:
64	
65	- **A public URL** — a Pages site, a deployed config, a published module, a live
66	  `/version.json` — files the **coded form**: declarative probes an agentless queue
67	  task (`claudinite-tasks/verify-production`) fetches and judges Action-side, where
68	  egress exists. No session ever runs, so there is no egress wall to hit — this is
69	  the lane for exactly the class that used to park. (3)
70	- **A GitHub read** — an issue's state, a file at HEAD, a workflow run's conclusion —
71	  files the **agentic form**: an unattended session on this repository, whose reach
72	  is narrower than yours — **GitHub, through its own tools, in the repositories its
73	  routine's scope names** — and nothing else. Take the read you are about to write
74	  into `Verify:` and answer, in one sentence, *which tool call the run makes, in
75	  which repository*. **Another repo is the standard trap**, because the read looks
76	  ordinary and the wall is invisible from here — a `Verify:` naming a member repo
77	  parks minutes after being picked, on a scope denial. (4)
78	  A cross-repo artifact with a
79	  public URL — a member's stamp on `raw.githubusercontent.com`, its Pages site — is
80	  not walled at all: it is a URL, and the coded form reads it.
81	- **Neither** — a login-walled console, a private dashboard, a repository outside
82	  scope with no public surface — **file nothing**: say in your reply that the change
83	  is unverified and what would prove it. That is a filter, not a fork: an unreadable
84	  artifact is a reason not to file. Filing anyway spends a session rediscovering the
85	  wall and then parks `needs-human-action`, which is the human's-memory outcome this
86	  skill exists to avoid. (3)
87	
88	Where the subject is the **fleet** rather than this repo — every member's stamp, every
89	member's CI — this queue is the wrong runner for it whatever you file. It belongs to a
90	routine that holds fleet scope, if the project has one, and to nobody otherwise.
91	
92	**Asking a person is the rare exception**, not the fallback. The bar is not "no
93	automatic check exists" — most changes clear that and still get nothing. It is that a
94	silent failure here would be **costly**, and you would be willing to interrupt the
95	person today to have them look. If you would not, the change goes unverified and you say
96	so. When it does clear that bar, file an ordinary issue — never a queue item: title it
97	the same `Verify in production: …`, carry `Original-issue:` and attach it as that
98	issue's sub-issue, and write the body per
99	[writing-handover-issues](../writing-handover-issues/SKILL.md) — somebody else runs it,
100	so the checklist is the artifact. **No mark, no
101	`Not-before:`, no `Retry-every:`, no `Model:`**: nothing in it is the queue's, and a mark
102	would buy only a session that parks. Assign it to whoever owns the release, and say in
103	your reply that you are spending their attention and why it was worth it.
104	
105	## What you file
106	
107	**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
108	the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
109	`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
110	verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. **Every field a run reads is one
111	block on the first lines of the description**, ahead of your prose — the same placement
112	[`/do-later`](../do-later/SKILL.md) files under, and what gives the retry below one place to
113	rewrite `Not-before:`. Then say what changed and why it could not be watched now.
114	
115	### The coded form — for a URL-readable artifact
116	
117	```
118	Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
119	Task: claudinite-tasks/verify-production
120	Live-probe: <url> :: <assertion that becomes true when the release lands>
121	Verify-probe: <url> :: <the assertion being verified>
122	Retry-every: <how often to re-probe while not yet live, e.g. 6 hours>
123	```
124	
125	The probes are the whole check, executed in code by the task the `Task:` line names —
126	no session, no `Model:`. `Live-probe:` is `In-production-when:` made executable and
127	`Verify-probe:` is `Verify:`; both classes are required, repeat either line for more
128	probes, and the assertion grammar (`status`, `contains`, `matches`, the `json` value
129	ops) is documented at its one home,
130	[`probes.mjs`](../../../claudinite-tasks/tasks/verify-production/probes.mjs). A
131	liveness probe failing re-arms the item by `Retry-every:`; a verify probe failing
132	against a live release reopens `Original-issue:` with what was asserted and what was
133	read; all passing closes the item with that evidence. No `Not-before:` is needed: a
134	coded run costs seconds, so probing from the moment of filing is the point, not a
135	waste — see the watch-it-fail step below.
136	
137	### The agentic form — for a GitHub read
138	
139	```
140	Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
141	In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
142	Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
143	Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
144	Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
145	Model: sonnet
146	```
147	
148	In either form, no `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has
149	already closed and there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.
150	
151	- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
152	  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
153	  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
154	  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
155	  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
156	  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
157	- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait.
158	  "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.basics` at 60906.12 or
159	  higher." "Any session started after this
160	  landed — check the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge
161	  is not a production condition, neither is elapsed time, and neither is anything the run
162	  cannot read.
163	- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read the run can
164	  actually make (the gate above): a file's content, an issue's state, a run's conclusion.
165	  "Issue #100 on that repo is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check
166	  the sweep works". A `Verify:` naming a person's step does not belong in this form at all —
167	  that is the rare human step above, an ordinary issue that never carries the mark.
168	- **`Not-before:`** is the queue's own wait field: adoption holds the run until the moment has
169	  passed. Aim it just past the release you expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
170	- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
171	  yet live, it re-arms `Not-before:` to **now + `Retry-every:`** — never the old value plus it.
172	  Size it to the release you wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in
173	  minutes.
174	
175	Then the mark, as `/do-later` applies it: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**, the one label the scheduler
176	run adopts — both forms alike. The agentic form's `Model: sonnet` is in its block because that
177	is the work: reading a live artifact and judging an assertion against it; the coded form names
178	no model, because nothing runs but code. Never `Automerge:` — a verification has nothing to
179	merge. If the mark doesn't exist in the repo yet, say so and leave the issue — it appears on the
180	next scheduler run.
181	
182	## Tell the agentic run how to converge
183	
184	The coded form needs none of this: its verdicts — requeue, pass, reopen — are the machinery's,
185	so its body ends with your prose and the playbook below would only be read as instructions by
186	something that takes none.
187	
188	For the agentic form, end the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole
189	brief, and the run decides nothing: it executes this playbook.
190	
191	**The transition off this issue is `converge-item.mjs`** — the command your instructions'
192	converge step names — **and never your own hand.** It reaches no network and needs none: it
193	reads the item you hand it, plans every side effect, and prints the calls for your own GitHub

195	that is what it is for, so there is nothing here to improvise. **Never write a

197	recorded nowhere the queue reads, and the done label then hides the item from the leash, so
198	nothing ever comes back for it. (5)
199	If the command refuses, it is telling you this item is not yours to converge — say so and stop.
200	
201	1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
202	   run, or elapsed time. If it turns out you cannot read it at all from here, that is
203	   `--outcome action`, naming the read and who can make it — not a silent walk-away.
204	2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: converge `--outcome done`, its `--summary` carrying the
205	   evidence actually read (the version, the value, the path); the command closes this issue.
206	   Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened
207	   instead and where you read it, then converge `--outcome done`, its summary linking that
208	   comment — the verification did its job by finding the fault, and the fault is now that
209	   issue's.
210	3. **Not yet live** → the one branch that converges nothing, because the run is not over: set
211	   `Not-before:` to **now + `Retry-every:`** — the instant you are
212	   reading this at, never the old value the field carries — **clear the issue's
213	   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
214	   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
215	   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.
216	
217	   Measure from the instant you read, because the queue releases a sleeping item on the
218	   first hourly pass past its moment, so by the time a run reads the field it is already
219	   behind — old + `Retry-every: 1 day` lands in the past again, the item goes ready on the
220	   very next pass, and a daily retry spends a session an hour. (6)
221	
222	## Then watch it fail, and say what you filed
223	
224	A coded verification runs for seconds, so its first execution is not left to faith: dispatch
225	the scheduler workflow (its `workflow_dispatch`) and
226	watch the first run report **not yet live** — proof the probes execute and fail for the right
227	reason instead of passing vacuously;
228	the same item then flips on its own once the release lands. A first run that *passes* before
229	the release you expected deserves a hard look, because a probe that cannot fail proves
230	nothing. The agentic form sleeps until its `Not-before:` and has no cheap forced run; filing
231	it correctly is the watch.
232	
233	One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: converge `--outcome done`, its `--summary` carrying the
   evidence actually read (the version, the value, the path); the command closes this issue.
   Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened
   instead and where you read it, then converge `--outcome done`, its summary linking that
   comment — the verification did its job by finding the fault, and the fault is now that
   issue's.
3. **Not yet live** → the one branch that converges nothing, because the run is not over: set
   `Not-before:` to **now + `Retry-every:`** — the instant you are
   reading this at, never the old value the field carries — **clear the issue's
   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

   Measure from the instant you read, because the queue releases a sleeping item on the
   first hourly pass past its moment, so by the time a run reads the field it is already
   behind — old + `Retry-every: 1 day` lands in the past again, the item goes ready on the
   very next pass, and a daily retry spends a session an hour. (6)

## Then watch it fail, and say what you filed

A coded verification runs for seconds, so its first execution is not left to faith: dispatch
the scheduler workflow (its `workflow_dispatch`) and
watch the first run report **not yet live** — proof the probes execute and fail for the right
reason instead of passing vacuously;
the same item then flips on its own once the release lands. A first run that *passes* before
the release you expected deserves a hard look, because a probe that cannot fail proves
nothing. The agentic form sleeps until its `Not-before:` and has no cheap forced run; filing
it correctly is the watch.

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.
